Read a table's rows

Source: R/read.R
lake_read.Rd

lake_read() returns the rows of a snapshot as a data frame. It prunes the live files with filter first, so that only the files whose rows could match are read, then reads each one with qio, adds the partition columns from the log, keeps the rows filter is TRUE for, and binds the pieces. lake_walk() does the same one file at a time and calls FUN on each piece instead of binding them, for tables larger than memory (but on Azure not larger than disk; see below).

Usage

lake_read(tbl, columns = NULL, filter = NULL, int64 = c("double", "integer64"))

lake_walk(
  tbl,
  FUN,
  columns = NULL,
  filter = NULL,
  int64 = c("double", "integer64")
)

Arguments

tbl

A snapshot, from lake_open().

columns

Columns to return, a character vector of column names, in that order. NULL, the default, returns every column qio can return.

filter

An expression over column names; see Details. NULL, the default, keeps every row.

int64

How 64-bit integers reach R, in data and partition columns: "double" (the default), exact up to 2^53 - 1 (qio returns NA with a warning past it, and a long partition value past 2^53 - 1 is an error of class zulake_error_int64), or "integer64" from the bit64 package.

FUN

A function, called with each piece: a data frame of one file's matching rows, in the same columns as lake_read() returns. Files without a matching row are skipped.

Value

lake_read() returns a data frame with one column per column asked for and one row per matching row, in the order of the files in lake_files() and of the rows in each file. lake_walk() returns NULL, invisibly.

Details

filter is an unevaluated R expression over column names, with values from the calling environment (a column's name always means the column). Its pruning subset is comparisons (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=), %in% and is.na() between a column and values, joined by !, & and |. That subset rules files out by their partition values and their statistics (minimum, maximum, null count and record count). Statistics only decide what is read: the rows returned are the rows filter is TRUE for whatever the statistics say, and a missing statistic only means a file is read. On a column returned as a list (a binary column), is.na() is TRUE where the value is null (NULL), as Delta means it, where base R's is.na() on a list is FALSE.

A filter may also apply these row-wise functions to columns: +, -, *, /, %%, %/%, ^, abs(), round(), floor(), ceiling(), sqrt(), exp(), log(), nchar(), toupper(), tolower(), substr(), startsWith(), endsWith(), grepl(), is.nan(), is.finite(), xor(), as.character(), as.numeric() and as.integer(); and compare two columns, or use a logical column alone. R evaluates those on the rows after reading (they never prune), with base R's functions whatever the caller defines, and each must give one TRUE, FALSE or NA per row. Before R 4.3.0, as.character(), substr(), toupper(), tolower() and grepl() of a timestamp or timestamp_ntz column are errors of class zulake_error_filter, since there a time's text depends on the other times formatted with it. Any other call with a column inside it, such as max(x), mean(x), rank(x), cumsum(x), duplicated(x), x[1], %in% with a column on its right, or a function of your own, is an error of class zulake_error_filter: a filter is decided row by row, so the rows it keeps do not depend on how the table's rows are split into files, and lake_read() equals the pieces of lake_walk() bound together. A part of the filter that names no column is a value, evaluated once where lake_read() is called, and may be any R expression.

Inside the pruning subset, comparisons are exact: a long, integer, short, byte or decimal column is compared with the value as decimal numbers, digit by digit, and a string column in UTF-8 byte order whatever the session's collation, as the table's statistics are. A value given as text, such as "12.30", is read as that decimal number; a double that is not the number its 15-digit form reads back as (1/3, 0.1 + 0.2) is an error asking for the value as text. R has already rounded a literal such as 9007199254740993 to a double (9007199254740992) before zulake sees it, so give such a value as text too. A float or double column takes only numbers: text there, such as amount > "100", is an error, since R would compare it with the column as strings. A date or timestamp column takes a Date or POSIXct, or text such as "2024-01-31" or "2024-01-31 12:00:00" (UTC unless it gives an offset).

Columns are typed as qio returns them (see qio::read_parquet()), and partition columns as lake_files() types them, except that a decimal of precision 15 or less, data or partition, is a double, which holds it exactly. An integer data value of -2^31 reads as NA, R's integer NA, with a warning from qio: is.na() is TRUE for it and a comparison such as x < 1 is not, and a file whose minimum may be -2^31 is never pruned on its null count. Columns zulake does not return are not lost silently: nested columns (struct, array, map), and decimals of precision above 15 until qio reads them exactly. With columns = NULL they are left out, each named in a warning of class zulake_warning_column_skipped (fields column and reason); named in columns or used in filter, such a column is an error of class zulake_error_column_unreadable with the same fields.

Data files are read in place on local disk. On Azure, every file left after pruning is downloaded to the session's temporary directory (tempdir()) before the first piece is read, by lake_walk() too, and kept there for the rest of the session, so that a later read of the same file downloads nothing. The disk used is the size of the files left after pruning: lake_walk() reads tables larger than memory, not larger than the temporary directory's disk.

Rows a deletion vector marks as deleted are never returned (see lake_deletion_vectors()); reading their vectors needs the zuroar package, and without it a read of a table with deletion vectors in the files it reads is an error of class zulake_error_missing_package. Every such vector is read and checked before any data file, so a corrupt one (zulake_error_corrupt_log) returns no rows. A table that maps column names (column mapping in name mode) is read by each column's physical name in the files and returned with its logical names; a timestamp_ntz column is a POSIXct in UTC.

See also

lake_files() to see which files a filter keeps, lake_count() for the number of rows from the log alone.

Examples

# The example table the package ships: orders partitioned by region, five versions.
path <- system.file("extdata", "orders", package = "zulake")
tbl <- lake_open(path)
head(lake_read(tbl))
#>   order_id customer amount order_date region
#> 1        3     Chen 980.25 2025-01-06   APAC
#> 2        6      Fay  75.75 2025-01-06   APAC
#> 3        9      Ivo 230.40 2025-01-06   APAC
#> 4       12      Kai  19.99 2025-01-07   APAC
#> 5       15      Mia  45.00 2025-01-07   APAC
#> 6       16     Chen  70.00 2025-01-08   APAC
lake_read(tbl, columns = c("order_id", "amount"), filter = region == "EU" & amount > 100)
#>   order_id amount
#> 1        1    120
#> 2        7   1500
#> 3       13    310
#> 4       17   2500
#> 5       20    330
# Row-wise functions filter rows; dates compare as dates.
lake_read(tbl, filter = order_date >= as.Date("2025-01-08") & nchar(customer) == 3)
#>   order_id customer amount order_date region
#> 1       19      Pia   99.9 2025-01-08   APAC
#> 2       24      Tia 1999.0 2025-01-10   APAC
#> 3       17      Noa 2500.0 2025-01-08     EU
#> 4       23      Ana   55.0 2025-01-10     EU
#> 5       18      Oli   15.0 2025-01-08     US
#> 6       21      Raj  820.0 2025-01-08     US
#> 7       22      Sam  410.0 2025-01-10     US

# One file at a time, for a table larger than memory:
total <- 0
lake_walk(tbl, function(piece) total <<- total + sum(piece$amount))
total
#> [1] 11615.79
